Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

something pronoun

also something or other, something new, something good, something useful

classical

Cic. Fam. 9.26.3: cotīdiē aliquid legitur aut scrībitur
Cic. Sen. 38: senīle aliquid … aliquid adulēscentis

aliquid

pronoun (neuter of aliquis)

“Something old, something new” takes an agreeing adjective or a genitive: senīle aliquid, aliquid adulēscentis (Cic. Sen. 38). A second-declension adjective is usually in the genitive (aliquid bonī, something good), a third-declension one agrees (aliquid ūtile). Lewis & Short (s.v. aliquis): aliquid says that the thing exists, though not which; quid leaves even that open.

Other words

  • quid — something, anything (after sī, nisi, num, nē)

    pronoun, declension · also used · classical · Col. 12.2.6: sī quid forte abest; Cic. Att. 15.16a: sī quid scrībere velīs

    After sī, nisi, num and nē the ali- drops: sī quid, if anything; nē quid, so that nothing.

  • nesciō quid — something or other

    also used · classical · Cic. Att. 13.38.1: exarāvī nesciō quid ad tē; Cic. Att. 9.10.1: hoc nesciō quid

  • quiddam — a certain something

    pronoun, declension · also used · classical · Cic. Sen. 33: nātūrāle quiddam; Cic. Leg. 3.23: quiddam malī (Lewis & Short)

Examples

  • sīc igitur vīvitur: cotīdiē aliquid legitur aut scrībitur

    so this is how we live: every day something gets read or writtenCic. Fam. 9.26.3

  • ut enim adulēscentem in quō est senīle aliquid, sīc senem in quō est aliquid adulēscentis probō

    as I like a young man with something of the old man in him, so I like an old man with something of the youngCic. Sen. 38

  • sī quid forte abest, ipse vacuus locus admonet, ut, quod deest, requīrātur

    if anything happens to be missing, the empty place itself reminds you to look for what is goneCol. 12.2.6

  • hīc nesciō quid bonī dēbet esse

    there must be something good in herePetr. 33.2

See also anything, everything, someone, what’s new?.
